articles.text: Ken Betts Suds Machine on Piedmont Avenue recently closed temporarily and will re-open in March, according to owner Carla Betts. The popular car wash, which includes a gas station, closed due to construction required by the state concerning gas station fuel storage. Betts is using the time to install new car wash equipment and ensure an even better experience for customers after renovations. California now mandates that single-walled storage tanks that store gasoline must be replaced with double-walled ones by the end of 2024. Betts says she chose to perform their renovations now rather than later because it resulted in the “least loss of sales,” compared to the rest of their year. Other gas stations owned by Betts did not require construction because they already had double-walled storage tanks. However, Betts admitted that factors outside her control may delay the re-opening of the car wash past March. The biggest obstacle to re-opening remains the lengthy regulatory processes required of the gas station site. “Some of the dirt at the site is contaminated as a result of the single-walled tanks. So, there have been lots of regulatory officials coming to check the dirt,” she added. Overall, Betts looks forward to re-opening as soon as possible. “We want the people of Piedmont and Oakland to come back when we reopen. We want the car wash to be the best it can be when that happens. When it reopens, it’s going to be a brand-spanking new type of car wash,” she said. If you would like to read it for yourself you can find it on page 162 of Parting the Waters: America In The King Years 1954-63, by Taylor Branch. It was January 1956 and the Montgomery Bus Boycott was in its second month. The tensions and demands Dr. King faced were immense. Because he was regularly receiving threatening phone calls, some his friends armed themselves and began to drive him everywhere he needed to go. There was also pressure from the boycott participants and community supporters. How long would the boycott continue? How much longer would their lives be disrupted? Was any progress being made? Were King and the boycott leaders up to the task or were they in over their heads? As historian Branch records the story: After another long day King buried his face in his hands at the kitchen table. He admitted to himself that he was afraid, that he had nothing left, that the people would falter if they looked to him for strength. Then he said as much out loud. He spoke the name of no deity, but his doubts spilled out as a prayer, ending, “I’ve come to the point where I can’t face it alone.” As he spoke these words, the fears suddenly began to melt away. He became intensely aware of an “inner voice” telling him to do what he thought was right. Such simplicity worked miracles, bring a shudder of relief and the courage to face anything. It was the first transcendent religious experience of his life…It confirmed for him his belief that the essence of religion was not a grand metaphysical idea but something personal, grounded in experience – something that opened up mysteriously beyond the predicaments of human beings in their frailest and noblest moments. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee invite the public to the 27th annual Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 15 from 11 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. at Piedmont High School’s Alan Harvey Theatre, 800 Magnolia Avenue. With a theme of Remain Awake, the event will feature keynote speaker Dr. Amber Johnson, Assistant Vice Chancellor and Chief of Staff in the Division for Equity & Inclusion at UC Berkeley. Also speaking are Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, and Piedmont Mayor Jen Cavenaugh. The celebration event will feature the Oakland Interfaith Youth Choir and winners of the Art & Essay Showcase. Four days before he was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee on April 4, 1968, Dr. King delivered a sermon at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C. Speaking about what he viewed as the evils of racism, poverty and militarism, Dr. King commented that “one of the great liabilities of life is that all too many people find themselves living amid a great period of social change and yet they fail to develop the new attitudes, the new mental responses that the new situation demands.” Dr. King noted that as citizens of one world, we are inextricably connected: “We are tied together in the single garment of destiny, caught in an inescapable network of mutuality. Whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly.” He issued the following challenge: “Let us stand up. Let us be a concerned generation. Let us remain awake through a great revolution.” Register to attend the event at: tinyurl.com/PADCMLK. articles.text: The magical experience of talking to grown-ups No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling mind blown when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world - from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up, the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share in. But that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good - it left them awed and they want to know how you felt while working on it Photo by Sebastián León Prado The relationship between a grown-up and child is very important. These adults made us feel like we were more than “just a kid.” Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. So how do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising coming from a camp director, but I recommend sending them to camp. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kid-at-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. and keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Affirmed. Interesting. Valuable. Creative. Loved. Special. Whatever wonderful feeling was felt, it was felt because someone took the time to help them feel the goodness that was already in themself. At Camp Augusta, we believe there is something awesome in every child. We need only to take the time to notice. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and program philosophies can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

articles.text: Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret, directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead. The Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close, explores the dark, exhilarating, and tumultuous life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms will not be in this production. More than 60 Piedmont High and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winning a Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. Sophomore Ben Wakefield expresses it well. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Shultz,” he said. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Performances are February 1, 2, 3, and 4 at 7:00 pm in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket.

The Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close, explores the dark, exhilarating, and tumultuous life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. articles.text: Victory over Berkeley, narrow loss to O’Dowd Staff Photos Brit Burden scored 29 points against Berkeley and 12 in a game with Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont’s boys basketball team returned from Winter Break by splitting its opening two Western Alameda County Conference games. The Highlanders lost by five points, narrowly 57-52, to Bishop O’Dowd at the Dragons’ home gym on Thursday, January 4. Two days later Piedmont defeated Berkeley, last year’s league champions, 66-55 at home in Binks Rawlings Gym. “Our game plan was great and our boys executed really well,” said coach Ben Spencer. “Our guys battled and rebounded really well. We played tough in the second half of both games.” The 11-point win over the Yellowjackets and former PHS coach Mike Hudson was a huge response to the loss at O’Dowd. The Highlanders have been doing it shorthanded without starting forward Declan Linnane in both games, and senior forward Alex Anderson suffering a season-ending injury in the first game of the season. “We’re down two starters and Dillon [Casey] was even dealing with the flu during the week. Our players battled and that’s all you want as a coach – to come out and compete,” said Spencer. “It was a tough loss to O’Dowd, it feels like we’re always so close to beating them. But it got us in the right mindset for Saturday’s game. We put up a fight and got good looks. It’s the next-man-up mentality; we have depth and everyone stepped up big,” said senior leader Brit Burden. Piedmont played tough defensive games against both O’Dowd and Berkeley, turning up the intensity after falling behind in the first quarter of both games. PHS trailed 14-13 in the early going against the Dragons, while they were behind 15-10 at the end of the first quarter against Berkeley. “We started playing with more energy. When we’re communicating on the floor, we play more as a group. We switched to a zone against Bishop O’Dowd, and we know when we’re in a zone that we’re all in it together. When one person is lagging it messes up the entire zone,” added Burden. 66-55 win over Berkeley Piedmont trailed 15-10 to end the first quarter but gained a 30-28 lead at halftime. The Highlanders then stormed ahead 49-38 in the third quarter, while both teams closed out with 17 points in the final going for the 66-55 victory. In Piedmont’s 20-point second quarter, sophomore Dillon Casey and Burden scored eight and seven points respectively, and guard Ravi Silverberg put up five. In the third, Burden dominated Berkeley on the floor with 12 points, driving into the paint for layups and field-goal attempts. Silverberg, meanwhile, had four points from the line. Burden continued to show his versatility with seven points including one 3-pointer in the fourth. Final stats: Burden scored 29 points, Casey had 22, Silverberg had nine, while Thorin Holmes and Lucas Malecki had three points. 57-52 to Bishop O’Dowd The two sides traded points in the first quarter with the Dragons leading 14-13 after a 3-pointer. But PHS took the lead at 18-17 going into the second. O’Dowd regained the lead at 34-32 at halftime, only to see PHS jump back in the lead at 42-40 going into the fourth quarter. In the fourth quarter, O’Dowd hit a pair of 3-pointers to lead Dillon Casey had 22 points in Piedmont’s win against Berkeley and led the scoring with 19 points against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Freshman Sebastien Swain was a breakout star on Piedmont High’s cross country team last fall, becoming the only runner at the school to qualify for the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park on Saturday, November 25. In doing so, he was selected for the All-State Freshman Team for Division 4 runners by Prep CalTrack on December 24. He was 67th of 201 runners at the state meet with a time of 16:41.3. His appearance at the State means Piedmont has sent at least one runner to the CIF Cross-Country Championship for 35 consecutive years. It’s something Swain didn’t entirely see coming once he first suited up in Purple and White. “It means a lot to me [to qualify for State]. I’m still really excited that I was just able to get there; it’s not something a lot of people get to do. It’s something I thought wasn’t even on the table before NCS when I qualified,” said Swain. From the first practice of the season, it was apparent Swain would be a standout runner in his debut year. “Sebastien showed up to our time trial before the season started and clocked the third-fastest time,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Sebastien has an impressive amount of poise and concentration when he is racing. We see it in practice and have observed this focus throughout the season.” According to Zirkelbach, Swain achieved a freshmen record for Piedmont High at Woodward Park, eclipsing Mark Ceraldi’s time of 16:59 set in 2003. “Seb’s performance was the 3rd fastest freshman runner in his race. He set the PHS Freshman record for the course, one that goes back 20 years to Mark Ceraldi in 2003,” said Zirkelbach. Distance runner Sebastien Swain was named to the AllState Freshman Team by Prep CalTrack. He finished 67th of 201 runners at the State Championship with a time of 16:41.3. Swain punched his ticket to State by finishing 13th of 140 runners with a time of 16:29.5 at the NCS Championship on November 18 at Hayward High amidst stormy conditions. He was also eighth of 38 in 16:22.13 in the WACC Championship, also at Hayward on November 4. Swain is currently competing on the boys’ soccer team and is expected to make the jump to the varsity track team during the spring. “I think he’s the real deal and has extraordinary potential,” said track coach Pouyan Assadi.

articles.text: Staff Photos Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills is considered an “ecological gem” because of its year-round display of blossoming plants. It has an ideal canopy for rain cover. With some rain in the forecast over the next week, looking out the window could be daunting for some hikers feeling those gray and gloomy vibes. But luckily for us in the Bay Area, there is a wealth of parks to choose from where hikers can avoid the wet weather with help of vast tree coverage. So grab your rain gear, hiking boots, and consider this group of five areas where you can enjoy some hiking even when it’s raining. Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve is a small treasure in the Oakland Hills. East Bay Regional Parks District (EBRPD) calls Huckleberry an “ecological gem” because of its year-round display of blossoming plants. The canopy of California Bays, Redwood trees, and Manzanita make it an ideal and small 3.4 mile loop. Manzanita trees, with their vibrant red burl, are currently in bloom. EBRPD has a list of plants currently blooming at the park. Redwood Regional A local favorite, Redwood Regional Park, is a default location for residents in the Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont hills. Several trails provide extensive tree coverage. Consider the French Trail, Chown Trail, Madrone Trail, Fern Trail, and Redwood Peak Trail as hikes that will put you beneath the canopy of trees. The West Ridge Trail provides an avenue where you can find each of the trailheads, parking at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area. Another connecting trail, which is well covered, is the Stream Trail, with parking at Canyon Meadow Staging Area. Joaquin Miller Adjacent to Redwood Regional Park on Skyline Boulevard, you’ll find trails with more foot traffic compared to the former, but equal amount of tree coverage along the Big Trees Trail, Sequoia Bayview Trail, Palos Colorados Trail, and the Sunset Trail. San Mateo: Purisima Creek Redwoods Traveling to San Mateo County; Purisima Creek’s Harkins Ridge provides a beautiful but rigorous journey through the hills surrounding San Mateo. Its trails beneath tree canopy are ideal for the rain. Consider the Purisima Creek Trail, which will go by the active Purisima Creek, where you can walk by large stumps of old growth trees with some second-growth trees scattered throughout the area. Marin: Cataract Falls Moving north to Marin County, the north end of Mt. Tamalpais has one of its most popular trails, the Cataract Falls Trail, where you’ll see a display of redwood trees towering over you. The rain will further enable the cascade of waterfalls along Cataract Creek, which will line your entire walk. Although less than four-miles, you’ll gain over 1,000 feet in elevation over steep steps and tree roots. It’s a perfect time to find mushroom while hiking on trails. Redwood Regional’s sprawling redwoods provide great cover from the rain.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is ringing in 2024 with the world premiere of playwright Minna Lee’s My Home on the Moon from January 25 through February 24. In this epic sci-fi journey into the metaverse, business is booming for a formerly failing Vietnamese pho restaurant in the middle of a gentrified neighborhood after it receives help from a mysterious marketing consultant. Things are not all they seem as the restaurant’s waiter, Mai, discovers that artificial intelligence-powered simulations may be taking over reality. With the help of her friends and family, and armed with delicious pho, Mai must learn to reckon the perfection of artificial life with the welcome imperfection of reality. A finalist in the 2024 Bay Area Playwrights Festival and semi-finalist at Ashland New Plays Festival, My Home on the Moon received developmental readings at UC Santa Cruz’s Rainbow Theater Festival and Denver, Colorado-based arts collective Bucharest Inside the Beltway. For tickets ($15-$100) and more information about the performance at SF Playhouse (450 Post Street), visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677-9596 Marketing consultant Vera (Rinabeth Apostol) learns the art of cooking pho from Mai (Jenny Nguyen Nelson) in the world premiere of My Home on the Moon at San Francisco Playhouse January 25 through February 24.

Hoyle began work on the show after the presidential election of Donald Trump in November 2016, working with increased urgency to complete the play as the American immigration debate continued to grow more polarized and heated on both sides. articles.text: Cult of Love will be performed by Berkeley Repertory Theatre from January 26 through March 3. Cult of Love, written by Leslye Headland and directed by Trip Cullman, will open at Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Friday, January 26, for a five-week run. Cult of Love is a ruthless comedy about a deeply Christian family, the Dahls, devoted to their belief that all one needs is love. The four Dahl siblings were brought up with a devotion to Jesus and each other. Now adults with their own distinct beliefs and years of emotional wariness, they gather once again for the holidays at their childhood home, singing joyous carols and recreate family traditions. However, repressed feelings and conflicts about the siblings’ upbringing shatter the family’s façade of forced cheer, and all hell soon breaks loose. Bold and provocative, Cult of Love dares to challenge our perceptions of family to examine what’s truly needed for deep faith and love to persist. “All families are inherently complicated, but in Leslye Headland and Trip Cullman’s hands, they are also dynamic, dramatic, and wildly entertaining,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “I’m delighted to welcome this incredibly gifted cast and creative team to Berkeley Rep.” Tickets ($22.50–$134) may be purchased at the box office or online at berkeleyrep.org/shows/ cult-of-love, or by phone at 647- 2949. Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theater is located at 2015 Addison Street.

articles.text: Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra to collaborate In an inaugural moment for the local music scene, two of Berkeley’s long-standing musical institutions, the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) and the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO), will join for a single performance, YPSO’s annual Winter Concert on January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church. YPSO proudly continues its 87th season, with Maestro David Ramadanoff celebrating an impressive 35 years as Music Director/Conductor. Leading a talented ensemble of 100 young musicians, ages 11 to 21 from cities spanning the Bay Area, from Napa to Pleasanton, Maestro Ramadanoff continues to inspire and guide the orchestra towards new heights. In a season brimming with activity, YPSO is performing the second of four subscription concerts, showcasing its talents at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, and embarking on a 9-day, 3-concert summer tour to Japan in June 2024. YPSO’s Winter Concert will feature works spanning three different centuries: Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum, the first movement of Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 featuring soloist Henry Stroud (winner of this year’s YPSO concerto competition), and Poulenc’s Gloria in collaboration with the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO), featuring soprano soloist Vuyiswa Sigadi. Bunch’s Supermaximum is a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination, in which Bunch draws inspiration from the reallife experiences of individuals facing extraordinary challenges. He has created a musical narrative that speaks to the strength of the human spirit. Following this, YPSO will perform the first movement. In program notes, Orrin Howard has written of Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61, “The first movement evolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” This piece will feature YPSO concertmaster Henry Stroud, a sophomore at Berkeley High, and winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. Closing the program is Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. It is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures. YPSO is collaborating on this piece with Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra, a longstanding Berkeley music organization led by Ming Luke (https://bcco.org/ upcoming-collaborations/). History of YPSO Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The 2023-24 season is its 87th. YPSO’s mission is to “encourage young people to become exemplary musicians and young musicians to become exemplary people”. The organization puts on four regular concerts per season. In addition, they reach out through programs such as Bread and Roses and the Bay Area Music Project to bring music into the lives of the surrounding community and encourage the civic development of its students. articles.text: ‘Seen’ by Laura Paladini to be the first ever curated exhibit at Alma Rise Alma Rise Gallery in Berkeley has announced its newest exhibition, “Seen,” will feature the work of Piedmont artist Laura Paladini. The exhibit, which contemplates the “enigma of invisibility” according to a press release, will open this Friday, January 12 during an opening reception from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m. at the gallery. Piedmonters may recognize Paladini from her previous involvement in the Piedmont Art Walk. She has worked with clients from her interior design firm in Piedmont for over 20 years. However in 2020, Paladini shifted her career focus to exploring the creative freedom of painting. Most of her work in recent years has been with oils on paper, wood panels, and canvas. “Laura was among the first artists I approached when we launched the gallery,” said Lupe Muller, the Executive Director at Alma Rise Gallery. Muller personally curated this show after being impressed by Paladini’s work. “I am personally really captivated by the authenticity embedded in her paintings and how she often shines a light on those we usually choose not to see.” “Seen” is an exploration of invisibility that examines societal norms, perceptions, and the ongoing struggle for recognition, something that resonates with Paladini personally. “I’m hoping that ‘Seen’ makes people examine the struggles other people are having, unseen, and that it presents them in a way that audiences can identify with,” said Paladini. Alma Rise Gallery is at 1600 Shattuck Ave, Suite 126 in Berkeley. “Seen,” will be on display from Friday, Jan 12 – Friday, Feb 9. Admission for this event will be free. No reservations are required for opening night. The show will be open every Saturday 1 p.m. – 4 p.m. or by appointment via email at info@almarisegallery.org. Artist Laura Paladini is shown next to a work titled His Domain, one of her most personal pieces featured in the new exhibition.

articles.text: Dan Flanagan and Trio Solano will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, January 13 at 7 p.m. The trio will performs string trios by Schubert, Sibelius and Beethoven, then will be joined by pianist Michael Seth Orland for Fauré’s epic Piano Quartet #1. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The film Extremely Loud/ Incredibly Close opens with what has become an iconic image of 9/11: the falling man. We bear witness to an individual dropping some 125 stories through the air, escaping a consuming fire but unable to escape the final outcome. Another image captured in the film, one that will forever be with us, is the scene of a brick wall. It’s only been a few days since the Twin Towers collapsed. In the dark of night, the camera slowly moves from right to left, revealing countless photographs of the missing, along with messages, many a plea to call home. At the foot of the wall are lighted candles and bouquets of flowers. In essence, the wall is a heartbreaking memorial to those who will likely never return and are lost forever amid the rubble and steel that now lies where the towers once stood. But there is more to this haunting and extraordinary film one that tells the story of a nine-year-old boy, Oskar Schell (Thomas Horn), who lost his father on what he refers to as “the worst day.” School had let out early on Tuesday, September 11, for reasons that are initially unclear to Oskar. He arrives home, and as usual checks the family’s message machine. Unexpectedly, message one is his father’s voice (Tom Hanks), a call from the 125th floor of one of the towers where he has been attending a meeting. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each building vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, instead observing the ceremony from a distance. A year passes and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when he is taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, Thomas Horn and Tom Hanks star in Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” Attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt. It was a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera to take their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud/ Intensely Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close. Directed by Stephen Daldry. Starring Tom Hanks, Thomas Horn, Sandra Bullock, Max von Sydow. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13. Made in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime?Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Coraline The stop-motion, animated feature Coraline is a tour de force of imagination. Made in 2009 in this reviewer’s hometown, Ashland, Oregon, it is a dark fantasy horror film written and directed by Henry Selick, and based on Neil Gaiman’s novella of the same name. Though made to be shown in stereoscopic 3-D, even in 2-D it is vivid and rich with a panoply of colors and strange and interesting characters. But, for all of its technical wonder and labor-intensive filming – the characters are three-dimensional figures that are moved ever so slightly, a single frame at a time – it’s hard to enthusiastically recommend this film for children. It is a sinister narrative which takes a young girl’s fantasy and turns it into a gothic nightmare. All fairytales have a distinctly dark side to them. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road only to meet the Wicked Witch. Alice falls down the rabbit hole into a world that is not simply benign. And certainly Harry Potter, for all of his deft ability with magic, encounters evil that takes many forms and threatens his very existence. And so it is with Coraline who has recently moved from Michigan to Ashland, Oregon. She and her parents have moved into a Victorian rooming house called the Pink Palace (remember the one in San Francisco in the 1960’s? This one, however, is filled with eccentric boarders. Feeling lonely and bored, and finding her parents distracted and cranky as they work intensely on a gardening catalogue (her mother is especially curt and preoccupied), Caroline explores the house and soon discovers a hidden door in her room that opens into a narrow tunnel (a rabbit hole?) and a parallel world. In this mirror universe, however, her new parents are attentive to her every need, and her room wonderfully inviting. articles.text: If there is genius in the stories of Nicolas Sparks, it’s that he writes with a deft understanding of his audience. From The Notebook to Message in a Bottle to Nights in Rodanthe, Sparks delivers wildly popular melodramas that aim to give the heart of the reader an emotional tug. He has to date written 14 novels. In the hands of a good director and screenwriter, his books make for solid, if formulaic movies that never fail to entertain. Dear John is directed by the talented Swedish film director Lasse Hallstrom, the husband of equally famous actress Lena Olin. Sparks’ story aims at tween and teen girls, and he nails it. I saw the movie on a Friday afternoon, just after school had let out for the weekend, and the theater was filled with teenage girls, all tightly packed in the center of the theater. This shouldn’t have been a surprise for Dear John stars two movie Channing Tatum as John Tyree, home on leave from his tour of duty with the Army’s Special Forces, and Amanda Seyfried as Savannah Curtis, a lovely, coltish college student, spending her spring break on the coast of South Carolina, near Charleston, where John lives. The time is late spring; several months before 9/11. Okay, the film is a Hallmark card. But that’s not a criticism. Sparks is a master at creating relationships defined by intense bonding, followed by separation, heartache, obstacles to unrequited love, a heart-wrenching surprise or two, and a denouement that generally satisfies. Savannah and John have an intense, glowing, sun-kissed two weeks together as they play and talk and cavort like two young seals in the gentle Atlantic surf. He is polite and withdrawn while she, in contrast, is open and direct. Their mutual attraction, however, is palpable. And through the lens of Hallstrom’s camera, all is soft, burnished, wrapped in an appealing yellow glow. Even the few war scenes are seemingly benign. Of course given the title of the film, John and Savannah will face a time apart, their only connection countless letters as John is sent around the world on classified assignments with his Special Forces team. Savannah, waiting, longing, goes to class, walks the campus, and decides that she would like to devote her life to working with autistic children (there’s an aside where she wonders if John’s father, played by the incomparable Richard Jenkins, might be mildly autistic). Recall that this is a melodrama. There will be roadblocks to John and Savannah being reunited, beginning with the 9/11 terrorist attack in New York City, and its impact on John’s time in the service. Though Dear John heads toward its inexorable climax, Hallstrom/Sparks will not make it easy. At one especially emotional point in the film (and there are many), young teens in the theater could be heard sniffing and trying not to breathe. For good reason. This is a nifty teen melodrama and there’s no doubt that those girls, filled with romantic impulses, enamored with the idea of love and finding a John themselves, will be swept away by this movie. These are the same girls that kept James Cameron’s “Titanic” afloat, so to speak. And they may do the same for Dear John. Dear John. Directed by Lasse Hallstrom, Starring Channing Tatum, Amanda Seyfried, Richard Jenkins and Henry Thomas. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming om VUDU/Netflix/Prime/Apple tv. Bring your yoga mat and pug and watch the pugs as they show you how to do a beautiful downward dog better than any human. The donation is $32 per human and pugs are free. Tricks & licks to all, –Jen and Rex, the Pug who loves yoga Dear Jen & Rex: That sounds like lots of fun and a few sore muscles, but it looks like it’s a pugs only event, so I can’t join you. Still, I looked at the site and I can easily donate to your pug mission. Thanks for letting us know. I suspect a lot of our plucky Piedmont Pugs will show their pug love for their fellow pugs-in-rescue and have a good romp at this party. What a hoot. A big bow wow to all. –Abby Dear Abby: What are the healthiest dog breeds? My dear dog-friend Turk just passed and I would like to avoid that feeling for a while. He lived to be nine…63 in dog years. Far too short. –Silvia Dear Silvia: I’m so sorry to hear about Turk. Getting a new puppy (or a new older dog) is definitely worth thinking through the health concerns that affect certain breeds. While I’m not sure if you prefer big or small review, but here’s the top three to get you started. 1. Australian Cattle Dog. We see these occasionally around Piedmont. The Guinness Book of Records says the World’s Oldest Dog was an ACD named Bluey, that lived to the ripe age of 29 in human years, 203 in dog years. 2. Poodles tend to have long, healthy lifespans of up to 18 years, regardless of whether they are Standard, Miniature or Toy. Eye and joint issues tend to affect them in their older years. 3. Border Collies tend to be lovable and vigorous and healthy for most of their lives which can be 12-18 years. Deafness and epilepsy can affect them when they get long in the paw. Certain breeds like bulldogs are known to develop respiratory issues. Pugs can commonly suffer from eye infections. Frenchies, which became the top U.S. dog breed last year, can suffer from excessive itching and licking as well as respiratory issues. Talk with other Piedmonters who own these breeds and they’ll tell you the true tale. Mutts and crossbreeds are commonly thought to be healthier than some purebreds, but there’s no guarantee that the dog you pick won’t develop something which turns into a hefty vet bill. Lots for you to chew on. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: Most wine historians believe that the first place on earth to make wine was the modern country of Georgia. The roots of Georgian viticulture have been traced back by archeology to when people of the South Caucasus discovered that wild grape juice turned into wine when it was left buried through the winter in a shallow pit. This knowledge was nourished by experience, and from 6000 BC inhabitants of the current Georgia were cultivating grapes and burying clay vessels known as kvevris in which to store their wine ready for serving at ground temperature. When filled with the fermented juice of the harvest, the kvevris are topped with a wooden lid and then covered and sealed with earth. Some may remain entombed for up to 50 years. With a diverse and unique microclimate, there are about 500 grape varieties in modern Georgia. Wine vessels of every shape, size and design have been the crucial part of pottery in Georgia for millennia. Ancient artifacts attest to the high skill of local craftsmen. Among vessels, the most ubiquitous and unique to Georgian wine-making culture are probably the kvevris, very large earthenware vessels with an inside coat of beeswax. Georgia ranks second (in terms of volume) in grape production in the former Soviet Union behind Moldova. Its wines had a high reputation in the Soviet Union. Currently, the wine is produced by thousands of small farmers (using primarily traditional techniques of winemaking), as well as certain monasteries and modern wineries. According to the Minister of Agriculture of Georgia, wine production has increased from 13.8 million 750ml bottles in 2009 to 15.8 million bottles in 2010. In 2009, Georgia exported nearly 11 million bottles of wine to 45 countries. Noted British Wine writer Oz Clarke writes the following about the wines of Georgia. “Georgia has preserved and cherished a wine culture more closely linked to its past than any of the other countries. It certainly makes wines whose tastes are completely, utterly removed from the experience of any normal modern wine drinker. And it uses methods of winemaking that you couldn’t invent in a modern world; you could only inherit them through the mists of time, maybe as far back as human records go.” I recently had the opportunity to taste some Georgian wines and was pleasantly surprised by both the quality and the originality of tastes. If your wine drinking has gotten into a bit of a rut, trying these wines would be a great way to break out. 2019 Marnaveli Rkatsiteli This is a light, refreshing white wine made from the Rkatsiteli grape and grown in the Kakheti region of Georgia. It reminds me of a Sancerre or a really crisp Chenin Blanc with abundant floral and citrus notes. It finishes clean and sharp and A typical Georgian wine cellar with underground Kvevri jars.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group had a good turnout of 33 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra on January 3 for their first walk of 2024. Piedmont students weren’t due back to school until January 8, so the walkers had a chance to walk the Piedmont High campus and see the construction progress on Witter Field. Walkers explore high school and Witter Field By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group had a good turnout of 33 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra on January 3 for their first walk of 2024. Piedmont students weren’t due back to school until January 8, so the walkers had a chance to walk the Piedmont High campus and see the construction progress on Witter Field. Some PHS history was shared. In 1916, Piedmont land developer Frank C. Havens was in financial trouble. He wanted to sell the Piedmont Park to raise funds. The Piedmont School Board wanted to purchase 13 acres of the park for a new high school, but Havens wouldn’t sell less than its entire 27 acres. The City of Piedmont wanted to save the park from development, but did not have money to purchase the remaining parkland. In November 1916, Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to purchase the land. The land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase 14 acres of the park if the City would reimburse them. The School District could buy the 13 acres it wanted and the City could have its park. Alexander purchased the land in 1921. One year later voters passed a bond issue and the City reimbursed Alexander and his partners. Construction began immediately on the high school in 1921 and Piedmont Junior High School was added in 1924. The walkers headed off for the high school. They took a path behind the Exedra along the top of the park that led them to a back entrance to the school. They walked down a breezeway to an open area in front of the Student Center and the Library. More PHS history was shared there. In 1974, the original school building was declared unsafe under state earthquake laws and was demolished, albeit with some difficulty due to the strength of the concrete. By the mid-2010s, this construction was also deemed earthquake unsafe and these buildings had to be demolished too. The school was reconstructed following voters’ passage of a “H1 Measure.” A new STEAM building and a new theater were built and opened in the fall of 2021. The school’s most famous non-graduate attendee is probably Clint Eastwood. According to research from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi, Clint excelled in P.E., but received poor grades in other classes. Classmates said he was interested in girls and cars. Clint attended PHS until January 1946, but transferred to Oakland Tech and graduated in 1949. The walkers continued past Millennium High School. It was established in 2000 at the start of the new Millennium. The group then went past the Binks Rawlings Gymnasium, and walked down “PE Hill” to Witter Field and the field house with lockers and offices for coaches. Standing on the balcony overlooking the field they could see that the new turf was in place with “Piedmont” written on it. The athletic field was originally added to the school in 1924. Witter Field was reconstructed and rededicated as the Witter Sports Complex in 1998 with a new synthetic turf field that was replaced in 2007. By 2023 this turf was worn out too. The field’s drainage also didn’t work well and the field often flooded in heavy rains. The repair price tag was $4,156,933. Thankfully, State Modernization Funds were available to pay for the project. They were like matching funds for Piedmont’s Measure H1 Bond. The group went down the stairs and walked over for a look at the baseball field. They circled back and checked out the relatively new, little-known field on Bern Court below the middle school. Piedmont Soccer Club got permission a few years ago to create this turf field for their youth practices. The walkers continued on past the PHS softball field to the lower entrance to Piedmont Park for their return to the Exedra. articles.text: When walking through Piedmont, it is interesting and fun to recognize, and try to name the various architectural styles employed in the homes and municipal buildings in town. As we have noted previously, this is in fact a big part of the aesthetic appeal of the place – the opposite of a large tract development all of the same architectural type. There are various reasons why certain styles were (and are) chosen for a building, including response to local climate, geography, material availability, as well as simply preference or architectural fashion. To begin with, because Piedmont lies on latitude 38, the same as the Mediterranean Sea, and because many early California settlers were from that area, it is only natural that the imported culture would include architectural inspiration from the surrounding countries, primarily Spain. Like a culture’s language and art, architecture is constantly evolving, constantly changing. It must, since “new” things like automobiles, appliances and superior construction materials and methods didn’t even exist when the styles we are still emulating first came into use. Although Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival are some of the names given to sub-categories of the Mediterranean Style family, it is well to remember that even the baseline style (“Spanish”) is only a snapshot of an architecture at one point in time, itself derived from previous iterations. Confusing? It can be. Architectural scholars can spot a certain type of detail on a building and know exactly how it fits into the historical timeline, but they often disagree on a number of things, including the various labels. But, back to the Mediterranean style. Although the variations share many recognizable characteristics (see photos), they all were, and continue to be, eclectic, meaning they are derived from a range of different sources. The basic Spanish architecture from which Mediterranean style is derived has itself been influenced by Moroccan, Italian, Portuguese, and French designs. One important overriding characteristic of this architecture is the informality. This is reflected in the relaxed asymmetry of the design, in both the plans and elevations (generally the more symmetry, the more formal the style). Another clue is the extensive use of inside/outside spaces. Any good work of architecture has a strong consistency between the exterior and interior design. In the Mediterranean styles, this is often reflected in high ceilings, exposed rough- hewn beams, textured plaster walls, and of course the continuation of the employment of arched openings. The floor plans are often L shaped, to form “enclosed” exterior courtyards, patios and terraces.
